I've been looking for a simple tool for getting new job postings from job boards, because I was tired of doomscrolling on the LinkedIn Jobs tab. Oh yeah, [sg]etting job alerts is equally overwhelming.^[Indeed's interface is annoying as hell anyway.]

Who to blame, but I've not found any that is "reliable", simple, and free.[^other-pkgs]

[^other-pkgs]: I tried [`jobspy`](https://github.com/speedyapply/JobSpy) for some time. However, the API is unstable and bundles unnecessary _downstream_ [dependencies](https://github.com/speedyapply/JobSpy/blob/fda080a373e8226f3fd60635323f5da9af9892b1/pyproject.toml#L19-L28) such as `pandas` and `numpy`. Unfortunately, it also appears not actively maintained. Nonetheless, `jobrake` owes a lot to `jobspy`.

::: callout-tip
I spend bonkers amount of time trying to "automate" my job search, but less on actually searching. So, heed my advice on this matter. 😅
:::

So `jobrake` (<a href="https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake"><i class="bi bi-github"></i></a>) is an ambitious attempt to address these challenges.

It's a simple CLI tool and Python package that fetches job postings from Indeed and LinkedIn and returns every result as the same small [`Job`](https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake/blob/main/src/jobrake/models.py#L30-L60) dictionary. There is no login, no browser automation, just simple requests via `httpx`.

I intend `jobrake` to be simple and light[^deps]. It searches, normalizes, and returns jobs. That is it. It helps you swing the rake at the big piles---LinkedIn and Indeed. So, currently, it does not support other boards such as Glassdoor or ZipRecruiter.

[^deps]: It depends on `httpx` and `beautifulsoup`. I leave it to you if you need downstream poking with the job search data with `pandas` and co. I had to point this because `jobspy` depends on lots of such packages.

## Installation

`jobrake` is not on PyPI so install it from GitHub with [`uv`](https://astral.sh/uv). Please read the [installation guides](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) for your system.

> _I assume unix-based systems hereafter, sorry Windows-(or dare I say WSL-) people, you're on your own---read the uv docs, adapt all the code wherever necessary; you can do it!_

I personally use `jobrake` through the CLI, so you can install it as a tool, too. `uv` installs `jobrake` and adds it to your `${PATH}`.

```sh
uv tool install git+https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake
# For ephemeral use
# uvx git+https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake
```

## A first rake

Say you're an _economist_ looking for _data science_ roles in the _Netherlands_, just like <mark>me</mark>^[<mark>Btw, seriously looking for a job. Hire me.</mark>].

::: {.columns style="font-size:0.9em;"}
::: column

```{sh}
#| label: linkedin-scraper
#| code-fold: show
#| code-overflow: scroll
jobrake linkedin \
        --query "economist OR data scientist" \
        --location "amsterdam, netherlands" \
        --max-age 24 \
        --results 5 \
        --output data/jobs-linkedin.csv \
        --details 2>/dev/null
```

:::

::: column

```{sh}
#| label: indeed-scraper
#| code-fold: show
jobrake indeed \
        -q "economist OR data scientist" \
        -c "netherlands" \
        -l "amsterdam" \
        -a 24 \
        -n 5 \
        -o data/jobs-indeed.json 2>/dev/null
```

:::
:::
_Note: If you're new to CLI lingo, left and right are the same interface twice: long flags spelled out for LinkedIn, and their short aliases for Indeed. Remove the redirect (`2>/dev/null`) to see progress updates and other info._

<details>
<summary>Expand for the results</summary>
::: panel-tabset
### LinkedIn
```{sh}
#| label: linkedin-output
#| output: asis
# The first three rows, some fields, description truncated
duckdb --markdown <<quack
select
    date,
    title: printf('[%s](%s)', title, url),
    company: printf('[%s](%s)', company, company_url),
    location,
    employment_type,
    applicants,
    description: regexp_replace(description, '\s+', ' ', 'g')[:500] || '...'
from 'data/jobs-linkedin.csv'
order by date desc
limit 3;
quack
```

### Indeed

````{sh}
#| label: indeed-output
#| output: asis
# The first three jobs, all fields, description truncated
echo '```json'
duckdb -json <<quack | jq
select * replace (regexp_replace(description, '\s+', ' ', 'g')[:500] || '...' as description)
from 'data/jobs-indeed.json'
order by date desc
limit 3;
quack
echo '```'
````

:::
</details>

By default, results are compact JSON on stdout:

````{sh}
#| label: default-stdout-output
#| output: asis
jobrake linkedin \
-q "data scientist" \
-l "london, england" -n 5 2>/dev/null \
| jq -r '"```json\n\(.)\n```"'
````

## Descriptions and other details

Every job result includes the same **identity** and **summary fields**, with `null` for unavailable summary values. **Detail fields** appear only when the job board supplies a value[^csv]. This keeps the common fields predictable, while keeping optional details compact.

[^csv]: However, if you request CSV via `--format csv` or `--output jobs.csv`, all fields appear as columns. 

The two sites differ in how much info they display upfront. Indeed includes every supported detail field in its search results. However, LinkedIn search cards contain only basic summaries, so `jobrake` "hydrates" them---fetches each posting page---when you ask for details such as the job description with `--details | -d`:

```sh
jobrake linkedin \
  -q "economist" \
  -l "amsterdam, north holland, netherlands" \
  -d
```

The difference also affects speed. Indeed searches are fast because we use its mobile app API. LinkedIn's guest search API is rate-limited, so `jobrake` uses a token bucket to pace requests. The LinkedIn scraper takes longer by design, so keep blinking at the progress bar.[^saying]
  
`jobrake` caches fetched details in your <mark>user cache directory</mark>. Repeated searches can reuse those details. If the cache is missing or damaged, `jobrake` fetches them again. Use `--no-cache` to disable caching.

[^saying]: Hey, let's talk LinkedIn at its own pace, as slow as we can. 😅 As they say, "_If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together._"

## Using `jobrake` from Python

Add it to your project dependencies with `uv`.

```sh
# create a .venv (uv venv .venv) or init a project uv init
uv add git+https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake
```

The package entry point is asynchronous:

```python
import asyncio

from jobrake import scrape


async def main():
    jobs = await scrape(
        "indeed",
        query="data scientist",
        country="netherlands",
        location="amsterdam",
        results=10,
    )

    for job in jobs:
        print(job["date"], job["title"], job["company"])

asyncio.run(main())
```

## What if ...?

::: {.callout-warning title="A caveat"}
Breaking in no time: Scrapers do not make promises, right? 🙃 `jobrake` pings unofficial(ly) (api) endpoints and relies on small HTML markups, so it lives at the mercy of LinkedIn and Indeed.
Changes of API endpoints or markups can break it any day. If a request fails, it's probably them, not us. [File an issue](https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake/issues), and offer fixes.
:::

The code is available at [github.com/eyayaw/jobrake](https://github.com/eyayaw/jobrake).

Happy searching, I mean, raking!

# Appendix {#appendix}

## Output formats

Explicit output-format selection:

```sh
jobrake ... --format json
jobrake ... -f jsonl
jobrake ... -f csv
```

Files still infer their format from the extension.

```sh
jobrake ... -o jobs.csv
jobrake ... -o jobs.jsonl
```

An explicit `--format` overrides that inference, i.e., you can do `-f jsonl -o jobs.txt` but you get JSON Lines in a `.txt` file.

## Place name resolution

`jobrake` can also resolve place names from the CLI. LinkedIn needs an unambiguous location to return results. Look up the place first, then use its display name in your search:

```sh
jobrake places linkedin "amsterdam"
# Then search with -l "Amsterdam, North Holland, Netherlands"
```

For Indeed, include the country:

```sh
jobrake places indeed -c netherlands "amsterdam"
```
